activities.anchor: a current account deficit means the country is losing money
activities.caption: benign or dangerous? trace the diagnosis
activities.name: itDeficitBranch

config.root: A country runs a current-account deficit of 8% of GDP. Trace whether it is benign or dangerous.

start.text: What does the deficit actually mean?

choices.label: The country invests or consumes more than it produces, financed by capital inflow
The country is losing money and will soon go broke
choices.feedback: A deficit is a balance, not a loss; the question is what finances it.

choices.label: Exports exceed imports
choices.feedback: A deficit means imports plus outflows exceed exports plus inflows.

meaning.text: What distinguishes a benign deficit from a dangerous one?

choices.label: What the borrowed resources build, and how durable the financing is
choices.feedback: Yes — capital goods and long-term local-currency debt versus short-term dollar debt.

choices.label: The size alone: any deficit above zero is dangerous
choices.feedback: The US has run around 3% for years; 8–10% is the red-flag range, but composition matters more.

choices.label: Whether the government or the private sector borrowed it
choices.feedback: That matters, but the use and durability of the financing matter more.

right.text: Benign: the inflow funds capital goods and durable financing, as South Korea's deficits did through its boom. Dangerous: short-term foreign-currency debt that flees at the first wobble — Asia 1997, Argentina repeatedly.

size.text: Scale matters — above 8–10% of GDP has historically been a red flag — but the sign alone is not the diagnosis.

broke.text: A deficit is arithmetic that must be financed, not a loss; the young United States ran deficits through the nineteenth century.

wrong.text: A deficit means imports plus outflows exceed exports plus inflows — the country is spending beyond its production, financed by capital inflow.

choices.label: What determines whether that is safe?

gov.text: Composition matters, but the use and durability of the financing matter more.

choices.label: See the test
choices.feedback: What it builds and how it is financed.

config.why: A deficit means investing or consuming more than producing, financed by capital inflow; judge it by what the money builds and how durable the financing is.

activities.anchor: Global value chains then scrambled the accounting
activities.caption: true or false — value added and the China shock
activities.name: itValueJudge

statements.s: Of the roughly $179 factory cost of an iPhone, only about $6.50 was value added in China.
statements.why: Assembly is a small slice of the value chain, however large it looks in gross trade statistics.

statements.s: Trade statistics that book the full assembly value as a Chinese export overstate China's value added.
statements.why: Gross exports double-count imported components; value-added accounting strips them out.

statements.s: Bilateral trade balances on value added look the same as gross trade balances.
statements.why: They can look very different — which is why much trade politics targets a statistic that no longer measures what it seems to.

statements.s: The China shock showed aggregate gains from trade are real and evenly shared.
statements.why: The gains were real; the losses concentrated in specific commuting zones for over a decade.
